column2: Judah descends from his brothers and reaches a particular Adullamite named Hirah. The separation and personal encounter remain; the temporal phrase supplies no exact calendar interval.

The feminine relative associates Shua's name with the Canaanite daughter in this selected Greek. Taking her and going in to her remain distinct; another tradition's allocation of the name is not substituted.
The woman conceives, bears a son and names him Er. Her grammatical agency in naming is retained rather than transferred to Judah without textual support.
A second conception and birth yield Onan, again named by the mother. Again reflects the explicit repeated action, not an ornamental narrative addition.
Another son is Shelah. The source says she was at Chasbi when she bore them, with feminine subject and plural object; neither is silently changed to a familiar alternate formulation.
Judah obtains Tamar as wife for his firstborn Er. Firstborn belongs to Er, while the named woman is Tamar; the English preserves these referents.
Er is evil before the Lord and God puts him to death. Both divine designations remain, and no unrecorded offense or medical cause is invented.
Judah commands intercourse, the brother-in-law duty and offspring for the deceased brother. The specialized marriage verb is explained naturally without importing an entire later legal code.

Whenever with the imperfect expresses repeated conduct. Onan's stated purpose is withholding offspring from his brother. Seed as the expelled substance is supplied contextually; no broader sexual doctrine is inferred.
The action is judged evil before God, who kills this brother also. Also connects Onan's fate with Er's; the candidate does not erase the stated causal evaluation.
Judah directs widowhood in Tamar's paternal house until Shelah grows, while fearing another son's death. Tamar's compliance follows. His fear is reported reasoning, not a narrator's endorsement.
After many days Shua dies, Judah is comforted, and he travels to shearing with Hirah his shepherd. Shepherd follows this Greek rather than a familiar friend label.
Tamar hears that her father-in-law is traveling to Timnah for shearing. The report preserves kinship and purpose without identifying an unnamed messenger.
Tamar changes widow's clothing, veils and adorns herself, then sits by Ainan's gates. Her reason is Shelah's maturity without marriage to him. The clothing term remains lexically provisional.
Judah considers her a prostitute because her face is covered and he does not recognize her. This is his inference, not the narrator's statement that she works in that occupation.

Judah turns aside and requests intercourse without recognizing his daughter-in-law. Her reply asks payment conditionally. The source's euphemism is retained without erotic elaboration or obscuring the transaction.
A young goat is promised from the flock, while Tamar requests a pledge pending delivery. Her elliptical conditional response is retained as dialogue rather than turned into an unconditional gift.
Ring, necklace and hand-held staff are the requested pledge. The necklace term and ring's exact function remain open; a seal cord is not silently substituted from familiar versions.
Tamar leaves, removes the covering and resumes widow's garments. The reversal of clothing is preserved, and no unexpressed judgment about her appearance is added.
Judah sends the goat through his Adullamite shepherd to retrieve the pledge; the shepherd fails to find her. The purpose belongs to the delivery, not to a newly narrated confrontation.
The shepherd asks local men about the roadside prostitute at Ainan, and they deny such a person was there. A cultic title is not imported into the ordinary Greek noun.
The shepherd returns and distinguishes his unsuccessful search from the inhabitants' denial. Both reports remain rather than collapsing them into a narrator's assertion about Tamar's whereabouts.
Judah lets her retain the pledges to avoid ridicule and contrasts his sending with the shepherd's failure to find her. The pronouns refer back to the objects and participants already introduced.

After three months Judah receives an accusation of prostitution and pregnancy and orders burning. The accusation and violent order are preserved as speech, without endorsement or an invented legal citation.
While being led out Tamar sends the identifying objects and requests recognition of their owner. The ring, necklace and staff recur individually, making the evidence connection explicit.

The perfect vindication verb with comparison supports more in the right than I in this dispute. Judah supplies his failure to give Shelah as the reason, then ceases sexual relations; no universal moral verdict is added.
At childbirth twins are present in her womb. The brief disclosure retains the timing and number without elaborating an obstetric sequence beyond the following verses.

One hand emerges and the midwife binds scarlet to it, expecting that child first. Thread is supplied as the natural material form; the source explicitly gives scarlet, not a detailed textile description.

Withdrawal of the hand precedes the brother's immediate birth and a barrier-breaking question. The name Perez follows. The difficult breach metaphor is retained provisionally rather than solved by an unsupported etymological paraphrase.

The scarlet-marked brother emerges afterward and receives the name Zerah. The English passive leaves the naming agent unspecified; the Greek's implicit subject should not be treated as a newly named participant.

Potiphar purchases Joseph from Ishmaelites and bears eunuch and chief-cook titles. These inherited labels remain provisional: their court-office senses need specialist evidence, and neither anatomy nor modern kitchen duties is certified by the glosses.

The Lord's presence accompanies Joseph's success within his Egyptian master's household. Prosperous here describes his activity despite enslavement; it is not a claim of independent wealth or freedom.
The master knows the Lord is with Joseph and prospers his work in his hands. The human master and divine Lord remain distinct uses of the same Greek title.

Joseph finds favor, pleases his master and receives household authority and entrusted possessions. The hand idiom conveys administration; the source does not say the possessions become Joseph's property.

After Joseph's appointment, blessing extends to the Egyptian's house and field for Joseph's sake. Both settings and the repeated possessions relationship remain, without a quantified prosperity claim.

The master entrusts everything and attends only to his own food. The second statement describes Joseph's form and appearance. The food exception's precise social meaning remains open rather than an assumed euphemism.
The master's wife directs her attention to Joseph and commands intercourse. Her active approach and his subordinate position remain clear; the candidate does not add a reciprocal desire.

Joseph refuses, then begins a conditional argument based on his master's trust and delegated possessions. The sentence continues into the next verse; no clause is detached to imply approval of the request.

The scope of Joseph's authority and the sole exclusion of the wife ground his question about evil and sin before God. Nothing above me remains syntactically provisional; authority need not imply superiority over the master.
Day-after-day speech and refusal are explicit. Sleeping with and the intercourse purpose remain represented; the source is not expanded into a separate rule about all nonsexual proximity.
Joseph enters for his work on a day when no household member is inside. The absence creates the setting without giving him an ulterior motive or inventing a festival.
She seizes his garments; he leaves them in her hands and flees outside. Plural garments is retained rather than normalized to one coat. The escape is his refusal in action.
Her perception of the abandoned garments and flight introduces her next response. The repeated escape details are preserved, and the verse intentionally continues syntactically into her summons.

Her accusation to the household calls Joseph a Hebrew servant and reverses the sexual demand. It is reported accusation, not a factual correction of the narrator; plural us preserves her appeal to the household.
In her account, her raised voice supposedly causes his flight and abandoned clothing. Beside me reflects her speech's wording, distinct from the narrator's in her hands.
She retains the clothes until the master returns home. The Greek historical present is naturally narrated in past English; the delay and location remain explicit.

The retelling to her husband includes a future first-person sexual assertion attributed to Joseph. Its wording differs from her earlier report and is preserved instead of harmonized into an exact repeated quotation.
She repeats the cry, abandoned clothes and flight as evidence. The candidate retains the allegation's sequence while the narrative context distinguishes it from the previously described events.
The master hears his wife's accusation and becomes angry. His anger's target is not explicitly specified in this clause, so the candidate does not supply one.

Joseph is cast into a fortress holding the king's prisoners. Fortress is repeated in the selected Greek; the candidate retains it without identifying a modern prison building or administrative institution.
The Lord remains with Joseph, pours mercy over him and grants favor before the chief jailer. Mercy and favor are separate terms; the fluid image is retained.
The jailer entrusts the prison, confined people and their activities to Joseph. The hand construction expresses responsibility rather than ownership or liberation of the prisoners.
The jailer need not supervise because all is through Joseph's hand and the Lord prospers his activity. The two causal relationships remain; the final statement echoes the earlier household success.
The chief cupbearer and chief baker offend their royal master. Both occupational titles and the Egyptian kingship are explicit; the offense itself is unspecified.

Pharaoh is angry with two eunuchs, identified as those same officers. The administrative/anatomical range of eunuch remains a lexical review issue; the number and offices are secure within the passage.
They enter custody with the jailer in the prison where Joseph was brought. The selected wording is preserved without importing the chief cook as the explicit custodian in this verse.
The chief prison official assigns them to Joseph, who attends them during a period of days. The exact title's relation to the jailer and chief cook needs historical lexical review.
Both dream in one night, each his own dream-vision. The distributive repetition is retained; it does not make their dreams identical, despite the shared night.
Joseph sees them troubled on his morning visit. Their emotional condition is reported without adding a supernatural cause or replacing it with a physical illness.
He asks why their faces are downcast today, identifying them as Pharaoh's officers in shared custody. The faces image and temporal today remain; ordinary you is plural.

The officers lack an interpreter; Joseph attributes explanation to God and invites their telling. Through God preserves the prepositional relation without claiming that Joseph supplies meaning independently.
The cupbearer begins with a vine before him in his dream. The reported vision's first-person viewpoint is kept, without treating the dream vine as an external historical object.
Three vine divisions, growth, shoots and ripe grape clusters appear. Branches is provisional for the base/stem term; the dream's compressed growth sequence is not rewritten as a botanical timetable.
Grapes are pressed into Pharaoh's cup and the cup is handed to him. The repeated cup and hand relationships remain, without adding fermentation or an explicitly named wine product.
Joseph identifies the three vine divisions with three days. The interpretation is explicitly his statement; the numerical mapping is preserved without extending it to every dream symbol elsewhere.
In three days Pharaoh remembers the office and restores its holder to cupbearing. Remember office follows this Greek, not an imported lifted-head idiom. The former service is explicitly recalled.
Joseph asks personal remembrance, mercy, mention to Pharaoh and release from the fortress. These linked requests remain distinct; the first does not by itself constitute a guarantee of release.

The emphatic stolen construction supports indeed stolen from Hebrew land. Joseph denies wrongdoing here and contrasts that with imprisonment. Pit remains his image rather than a newly measured underground location.

The baker regards the interpretation as right and reports three baskets of coarse bread on his head. The grain/bread term is unresolved; neither white bread nor a specific flour species should replace it without lexical evidence.
The top basket has varied royal baker's food, which sky-birds consume. The food, baker's work and overhead position remain; no recipe or particular pastry is invented.
Joseph identifies the three baskets with three days, paralleling the prior interpretation. The same number does not imply the same outcome, which is stated in the next unit.
The future prediction removes the head, hangs the man on wood and exposes his flesh to birds. Tree is inherited for wood; exact execution hardware is not independently established.
The third day is Pharaoh's birthday, with a drinking feast and remembrance of both offices among his servants. The drinking element and paired administrative positions are retained.
The cupbearer is restored and gives Pharaoh the cup. The second clause shifts its acting subject back to the officer naturally; it does not describe Pharaoh handing himself a cup.
The baker is hanged in accordance with Joseph's interpretation. The concise fulfillment statement is not expanded into execution details from the earlier prediction.
The cupbearer fails to remember Joseph and forgets him. The apparent redundancy is meaningful narrative closure and is retained rather than reduced to one clause.
Two full years precede Pharaoh's dream of standing by the river. Full expresses the years-of-days formula. The river is unnamed here; Nile is not newly inserted.
Seven attractive, well-fleshed cows emerge as though from the river and graze in the marsh growth. Reeds is a provisional botanical rendering; the dreamlike as though remains.
Seven other cows follow, ugly and lean, grazing alongside the first at the bank. The contrasting two descriptions and common location remain distinct.
The lean ugly cows devour the attractive choice cows, and Pharaoh wakes. The number seven is retained for both groups; the extraordinary action remains a dream event.
The second dream has seven good choice ears on one stalk. Grain is supplied to disambiguate English ears; the source does not specify a modern crop variety.
Seven thin wind-damaged ears sprout afterward. Wind-blighted preserves the compound without importing an eastward direction or a named meteorological system.
The thin wind-damaged ears swallow the full choice ears. Awakening and recognition as dream remain; the narrative is not rationalized into ordinary crop loss.
Pharaoh's troubled soul leads to summoning all interpreters and wise men, none of whom explains the dream. Interpreters avoids adding a magical occupational label absent from this noun.

The cupbearer recalls his offense today. Singular offense is retained; whether it emphasizes the earlier royal offense or forgetting Joseph remains contextual interpretation rather than a new explicit object.
His account places both officers in custody at the chief cook's house. That title remains consistent with the inherited rendering, with its ancient official sense still requiring review.
He and the baker dream during one night, each according to his own dream. The individual experiences and shared timing remain; the narrative is not compressed into one identical dream.
Joseph is described as a young Hebrew servant of the chief cook who interprets after hearing them. Youth, ethnicity and service relation are separate; the title is not silently modernized.
The account stresses agreement between interpretation and outcome: one restored to office, the other hanged. The two infinitival outcomes are clearly assigned in the English.
Unnamed plural attendants bring Joseph out, shave him and change his clothing before his audience. The candidate preserves their agency rather than making every preparation a reflexive act by Joseph.

Pharaoh recounts an uninterpreted dream and hearsay about Joseph's ability after hearing dreams. The reported claim is distinguished from the narrator's direct certification of unlimited interpretive power.

The negative depends on apart from God, followed by difficult deliverance/answer syntax. The inherited answer bringing deliverance is a contextual interpretation, not a resolved parse. It must not be replaced by a familiar peaceful-answer formula without evidence.

Pharaoh's own report situates him beside the riverbank in his dream. The first-person retelling is retained separately from the initial third-person account rather than silently harmonized in wording.
The seven attractive well-fleshed cows and marsh grazing recur in Pharaoh's report. The as though construction remains; the plant rendering requires the same caution as 41:2.
The second group is wretched, ugly and lean beyond Pharaoh's prior experience in Egypt. His comparative claim is retained as his speech, not a zoological record.
The later cows consume the first seven, described again as fair and choice. First marks the earlier group, while the repeated adjectives reinforce the contrast.
Consumption leaves no visible improvement; the repeated belly image and former ugliness remain. Awakening followed by renewed sleep is included within the inherited unit, preserving its sequence.
Pharaoh again sees seven full good ears on one stalk. Again is explicit here. The stalk term remains consistent with 41:5 without introducing a botanical species.

The later seven ears are thin and wind-blighted, growing adjacent/following the first. Beside is the inherited contextual rendering of the attached sequence; the relationship merits lexical precision review.
The damaged ears swallow the good full ears, and the interpreters fail to explain it. The narrative retains Pharaoh's act of telling them rather than reducing their inability to a generalized maxim.
Joseph says the dream is one and God has shown His action to Pharaoh. About to do is contextual for the present in a predictive dream; the candidate does not claim a separate future-tense form.
Seven cows and seven ears each represent seven years, followed by the repeated unity statement. The mapping is not doubled into fourteen years of plenty.
The seven later lean cows and seven wind-blighted ears correspond to seven famine years. The future in the final clause is retained; the paired symbols denote one period.
Joseph restates his explanation that God showed Pharaoh His intended action. The repeated proposition remains rather than being removed for stylistic variety; its predictive force comes from context.
Seven years of great abundance are coming throughout Egypt. The whole-land scope and great degree remain, without an imported yield percentage.
Seven famine years follow, erasing remembrance of plenty and consuming the land. The undefined plural they is kept naturally; no additional named population is supplied.
The later famine's great severity prevents recognition of the former abundance. The explanatory because clause is retained rather than converting the relation into a new prediction of depopulation.
The doubled dream means the word from God will be true and God will hasten its execution. True follows this Greek; the rendering is not silently replaced by an alternative established formulation.
Joseph commands consideration of a prudent, discerning man and his appointment over Egypt. Both qualities remain; a modern ministerial title is not supplied.
Pharaoh is to act and appoint local governors, who take a fifth of all produce during the seven abundant years. The one-fifth levy is explicit in the verb; no modern tax policy is inferred.

Officials gather food, grain is placed under Pharaoh's authority, and food is stored in cities. Hand is the administrative image. The injunction is preserved alongside the preceding fifth, without resolving policy detail by deleting all.

Stored food is for the land through seven famine years to prevent its destruction. The reserve's duration and protective purpose remain; the verse does not promise unlimited supplies beyond that period.
Joseph's words please Pharaoh and all his servants. Approval is explicitly collective. It is not yet the appointment itself, which occurs through the following exchange.
Pharaoh asks about finding such a man with God's spirit in him. The inherited capitalization is editorial; the anarthrous phrase is not treated as independently proving a later doctrinal formulation.
Pharaoh reasons from God's disclosure to Joseph's exceptional prudence and discernment. The comparative qualities repeat the proposed criteria. The statement is Pharaoh's appraisal in the scene.

Propose obey your command for the metonym obey at your mouth. Mouth expresses authoritative speech here; command makes it intelligible in English while the throne alone remains Pharaoh's exception. The literal image stays recorded as an alternative.
Pharaoh explicitly appoints Joseph today over all Egypt. The performative present is kept. Today and all are source features, not added emphasis.

Pharaoh transfers his ring, dresses Joseph in fine linen and places a gold collar around his neck. The three investiture objects remain; their exact administrative symbolism is not inserted into Scripture.
Joseph rides the second chariot and a herald proclaims before him. The selected Greek gives no quoted cry, so a familiar bow-the-knee command is not imported. Appointment over Egypt is repeated.
Pharaoh asserts his identity and prohibits anyone lifting a hand without Joseph. The Greek mentions hand only, so foot is not supplied. The scope is all Egypt; the idiom concerns authorized action.

Joseph receives the selected Greek form Psonthomphanech and Asenath, daughter of Heliopolis's priest. Existing spellings are retained; no unsupported Egyptian etymology or identification with the earlier Potiphar is asserted.
Joseph is thirty at his audience with Pharaoh and then travels throughout Egypt. The age belongs to the appointment period, not his earlier enslavement. The two movements remain distinct.
The land produces sheaves/handfuls during the seven abundant years. Sheaves is provisional for the agricultural noun; no unsupported yield multiplier is supplied.
Food of all seven abundant years is stored city by city from surrounding fields. The local collection relationship remains, without substituting a single centralized granary in one capital.
Grain accumulates like sea-sand until counting fails. The plural inability to count is retained; the simile conveys uncountability rather than a literal infinite quantity.
Two sons are born before the famine to Asenath, whose paternal and priestly connections recur. The full identification remains despite repetition, and the births are not assigned unrecorded dates.
Manasseh's naming explanation concerns forgotten toil and all his father's things/affairs. Affairs is an English supply for the elliptical possessive; the text does not explicitly say household here.
Ephraim's explanation uses increased me in the land of humiliation. Both the increase verb and difficult life setting remain. The name is not replaced by an explanatory English label.
The seven abundant years in Egypt pass away. The completed period remains distinct from the coming famine, and no overlap is added to compress the chronology.

Famine begins as Joseph said and affects the land broadly, while Egypt has bread. The contrast is preserved without asserting that Egypt's population experiences no hunger whatsoever in the next verse.

Egypt's hunger leads to an appeal for bread, and Pharaoh directs everyone to Joseph's instructions. Food availability and access are distinct in the narrative; the candidate does not erase the tension.
Joseph opens all granaries and sells to all Egyptians amid widespread famine. Sales are explicit, not free distribution. The scope expression is preserved without a new global geography claim.
All countries come to buy because famine prevails broadly. Countries is a collective designation for their people; the translation does not invent a complete list or census of every nation.
Jacob learns of available sale in Egypt and asks why his sons are idle. Grain supplies the commodity from context. Idle follows the Greek rather than a familiar question about looking at one another.
He reports hearing of grain, commands descent and purchase of a little food, and gives survival as the purpose. Live and not die are both retained.
Joseph's ten brothers descend to purchase grain from Egypt. The explicit ten excludes Benjamin in the following explanation; the number is not inferred solely from later narrative.
Benjamin is withheld because Jacob fears sickness may befall him. Sickness follows the selected noun; generic misfortune is not substituted without noting the lexical difference.
Israel's sons join other buyers because Canaan is famine-stricken. The collective flow and causal explanation remain, without an invented border restriction.
Joseph governs and sells grain to the land's people; his brothers bow with faces to earth. The two administrative functions and the act of homage remain separate.
Joseph recognizes them, acts as a stranger and speaks harshly before asking their origin. Their answer states Canaan and food purchase. The concealment is deliberate behavior, not failed recognition.
Recognition is explicitly one-sided. The repeated statement reinforces dramatic irony, so it is retained instead of deleted as stylistic redundancy.

Joseph recalls his dreams and accuses the brothers of inspecting the country's tracks. Tracks is a provisional lexical choice; familiar nakedness or defenselessness imagery is not substituted into this selected Greek.
They deny the charge and identify their purpose as buying food, addressing Joseph deferentially. Ordinary your correctly refers to a human superior rather than requiring divine archaism.
One father and peaceable character support their denial of spying. Peaceable follows the selected adjective; honest may be related contextually but is not silently substituted.
Joseph rejects their account and repeats the accusation about seeing the land's tracks. The same unresolved territorial term remains consistent with 42:9.

They describe twelve brothers, with the youngest presently at home and another no longer existing. The last expression is kept indirect; it is not changed into a narrator's confirmation of Joseph's death.
Joseph treats their explanation as confirming his earlier accusation. The repeated spies quotation is preserved as his argument, without making it the narrator's verdict.

The test invokes Pharaoh's health and emphatically prohibits departure until the youngest arrives. Health is retained rather than changed to life; the oath does not become a narrator's religious endorsement.

One brother is to fetch the youngest while the others are detained until truth is established. The negative alternative repeats the oath and accusation. The plan is distinct from the later reduced detention.
The whole group is placed in custody for three days. The duration is explicit and precedes the third-day proposal, not a separate three-day journey.
Joseph introduces the revised instruction with a survival promise and his fear of God. The causal aside belongs to his speech; it is not expanded into disclosure of his identity.
If peaceable, they leave one brother detained and carry purchased grain home. The retained singular hostage differs from the earlier plan to detain the others; that change is preserved.

Bringing the youngest establishes credibility; failure means death. The selected Greek explicitly includes the negative alternative. The compliance statement is retained without implying Benjamin has already arrived.
Each brother acknowledges sin over disregarding the other's distress and pleas, linking it with their current distress. The repeated affliction language remains; the causal interpretation is theirs.
Reuben recalls his warning and their refusal to listen, then says the brother's blood is being required. The accountability image remains without naming a new explicit avenger.
They do not know Joseph understands because an interpreter stands between them. Understood is contextual for hearing; it does not claim a different Greek verb for cognition.
Joseph turns away to weep, returns, speaks and binds Simeon in their presence. The narrative preserves both private emotion and public detention without inventing the unquoted speech.
Joseph orders filled vessels, each person's silver returned to his own sack and journey provisions. The individualized repayment and separate travel food remain; the brothers' knowledge is not added.
They load grain on their donkeys and depart. The commodity and transport animals are explicit; no unrecorded change of cargo quantity is inferred.
One brother opens his bag to feed his donkeys and sees bundled silver at its mouth. The singular discoverer and plural donkeys are retained; he is not named without evidence.
He announces the returned silver; the group reacts with astonishment and disturbance and asks what God has done. Their question remains an interpretation of events, not a new revelation.

The brothers return to Jacob in Canaan and report everything that befell them. The introduction continues into direct speech; the broad everything is not a claim that every earlier detail is quoted verbatim.
Their report describes harsh speech and imprisonment as supposed spies. The selected Greek's custody clause is retained instead of shortened to an accusation alone.
They recount their peaceable status and denial of spying. The English preserves the same recurring adjective as the original dialogue, supporting the report's verbal links.
The retelling again lists twelve brothers, one absent and the youngest with the father in Canaan today. The father's relationship and present timing remain rather than a reconstructed genealogy.

The ruler's quoted test leaves one brother while the others take purchased household food. Household provision is explicit in this retelling, and its wording is not forced into exact identity with 42:19.
Producing the youngest verifies peaceable intent, frees the detained brother and permits trade. The final commercial clause is preserved; it is not reduced to a general permission to travel.
All sacks reveal their individual silver bundles, and both sons and father fear. This fuller discovery remains distinct from the single brother's earlier discovery during travel.
Jacob laments bereavement, Joseph and Simeon being absent, and the prospective loss of Benjamin. His no-more statements express his situation and fear; they do not establish that Simeon is dead.
Reuben offers his two sons' lives as a guarantee and asks custody of Benjamin. The disturbing proposal remains reported speech, without endorsement or substitution of a milder pledge.

Propose restoring the future assertion: he will fall sick on the way. The Greek here has a future rather than the inherited if-clause; it expresses Jacob's feared prediction, not the narrator's certainty. Old age, sorrow and Hades remain.
The famine intensifies in the land. The simple report advances the pressure behind the next request; no new location or quantified shortage is supplied.
After the Egyptian grain is consumed, the father orders another small food purchase. Again and the completed eating are explicit; the sequence does not imply an immediate same-day return.
Judah recalls an emphatic warning that access to the ruler's face requires the youngest brother. Solemnly warned represents the cognate emphasis. Face remains a clear audience idiom here.
Judah makes travel and purchasing conditional on their father's sending the brother. The food is for the father/household; the condition is not rewritten as an unconditional refusal.
The negative alternative repeats the warning and refusal to go without the brother. Repetition is retained because it grounds Judah's stance, rather than removed as redundant dialogue.
Israel accuses them of harming him by disclosing another brother. The question reflects his grievance, not a narrator's judgment that their disclosure was wrongdoing.
The brothers report close questioning about family, father's survival and another brother, then disclaim foreknowledge of the demand. The rhetorical question and repeated inquiry remain.

Judah requests the lad's company for the survival of brothers, father and household group. Households is contextual for the dependents/baggage term; the precise social scope remains a lexical question.

Judah personally accepts responsibility and lasting guilt if he fails to return Benjamin before Jacob. Surety conveys the undertaking in context; the hand image and permanent accountability are retained.
The past counterfactual says they could already have returned twice without delay. Twice is explicit and not flattened into merely long ago.

Propose incense rather than spices for the selected fumigation noun. Resin, honey, stacte, terebinth and nuts remain distinct; botanical identities and stacte's precise substance remain unresolved rather than replaced with familiar alternative plants.
They must take double silver and return the earlier money, allowing that it may be an oversight. Perhaps preserves uncertainty; the father is not asserting that he knows how the money returned.
The instruction adds taking the brother and rising to descend to the man. The repeated travel command remains linked to the negotiated condition and prepared gifts.
Jacob wishes favor from my God and release of the detained brother and Benjamin, then acknowledges bereavement. My God follows the selected Greek; an Almighty title is not added.
The men take the gifts, double silver and Benjamin and stand before Joseph. Each element of Jacob's instruction is represented without adding an unrecorded exchange en route.

Joseph recognizes Benjamin as his same-mother brother and orders hospitality, slaughter and a noon meal. The slaughter noun is not automatically made a cult sacrifice. Steward describes the man over the house contextually.
The steward obeys and brings the group into Joseph's house. The action is reported before their interpretation, preserving the contrast between hospitality and their suspicion.

The brothers fear false accusation, assault and enslavement connected with the returned silver, including seizure of donkeys. These are their suspicions, not the narrator's account of Joseph's intended treatment.
They approach the man over Joseph's house at its gateway. Their explanatory speech begins in the next unit; location and official role remain distinct.
They open deferentially and identify the first journey's food-purchase purpose. Ordinary lord is human address, with no divine-pronoun change.
Their report says each person's silver was discovered at lodging and is returned by weight. Full weight is contextual for repayment; no coin count or modern monetary value is supplied.
They distinguish additional purchase money from the returned sum and deny knowing who placed it. The denial is preserved despite the reader's earlier knowledge of Joseph's order.

The steward reassures them, attributes their treasure to their ancestral God and acknowledges receipt of acceptable silver, then releases Simeon. The exact commercial force of good/in-full merits lexical review; no additional payment is invented.
Water for washing feet and fodder for donkeys are provided. The purpose infinitive does not explicitly identify who washes the feet; the candidate leaves the practical agent open.

They prepare gifts before Joseph's noon arrival because they hear he will dine there. The selected singular dining reference is retained rather than silently changed to an explicit promise about their own meal.
Joseph enters, receives the hand-carried gifts and the brothers' face-to-earth obeisance. The repeated house and hand relationships remain without inserting an unrecorded acceptance speech.
Joseph asks their welfare and the aged father's health and continued life. The separate questions are retained instead of compressed into a single general greeting.
They answer that their father lives; a blessing of that man follows in the selected Greek, then renewed bowing. The extra blessing is preserved, with its implicit speaker left pronominal.
Joseph identifies his same-mother brother and asks whether this is the promised youngest, then wishes divine mercy. Child is affectionate address and does not establish Benjamin's numerical age.
Joseph's inward organs are stirred toward his brother, prompting private weeping. Inward parts preserves the bodily emotion image; no clinical diagnosis is attached to it.
He washes his face, returns, restrains himself and orders bread served. The sequence separates his private emotion from public composure without erasing either.

Joseph, brothers and Egyptians dine separately, with the narrator explaining an Egyptian aversion to shared bread with Hebrews. The statement is contextual ancient narration, not a generalized present-day claim.
They sit by birth order and marvel at one another. The eldest/youngest contrast expresses ordered ages; the candidate does not add an unrecorded announcement of their names.

Benjamin's portion is fivefold compared with the others; they drink and become drunk with Joseph. The intoxication verb is retained instead of euphemized as merely cheerful, without a claim about exact alcohol quantity.

Joseph addresses the household steward using plural fill/put commands for the serving group. Sacks receive all they can carry and individual silver at each mouth. Ordinary English you leaves number implicit here.

Joseph's silver cup and the youngest's grain payment are placed in that sack. The cup is specifically his and silver; no later divination interpretation is imported into the object description itself.
At dawn the men and their donkeys are dismissed. The passive does not name an additional dismissing agent, and the morning sequence continues from the prior preparations.
After departure but before much distance, Joseph orders pursuit and an accusation of repaying evil for good. The charge is a scripted test in context, not narrator-certified theft.

The selected speech retains my cup followed by my lord, a difficult quoted voice shift. Drinking and emphatic divination are both present. Their occurrence in the accusation does not independently certify Joseph's habitual practice.
The steward finds the brothers and delivers the prescribed words. The fulfillment is kept concise without inventing additional threats or explanation of the planted cup.
They question the accusation and strongly deny such conduct by the servants. The negative wish is idiomatically Far be it, not a literal prediction of what cannot happen.
Their return of silver from Canaan grounds the rhetorical question about stealing silver or gold. The two metals remain, and the hypothetical question is not a confession.

They rashly propose death for the cup-holder and slavery for themselves. The cup is explicit in this selected reading; the proposal is preserved without endorsement or alteration into a lawful sentence.
The steward responds by limiting slavery to the cup-holder and clearing the rest. Despite as you say, his condition differs from their death offer; the translation preserves the actual distinction.
Each brother hurries to lower and open his own sack. The distributive each is repeated, accounting for the individualized search rather than a collective pile of unspecified bags.

The search proceeds eldest to youngest and finds the cup in Benjamin's sack. The order and discovery remain explicit; the narrator has already established planting, so discovery is not proof of voluntary theft.
All tear their clothing, reload individual donkeys and return to the city. The collective mourning and personal reloading are both preserved without adding spoken lament.
Judah and brothers enter before Joseph, who remains there, and fall to the ground. Judah's named lead is retained; the others are not omitted from the action.

Joseph questions their deed and claims emphatic divining ability for a man like himself. The contextual claim is preserved rather than rationalized or treated as independent confirmation of occult activity.

Judah asks how to answer, speak or be justified, then acknowledges God finding their injustice and offers all as slaves. The legal-vindication question is contextual; a doctrinal theory of justification is not inserted.

Joseph rejects collective enslavement, retaining only the cup-holder and sending the rest safely to their father. Safety follows the selected noun and is not silently replaced by a different farewell formula.
Judah requests speech and restraint of anger, recognizing Joseph's position next to Pharaoh. The prepositional rank expression is retained rather than changed to exactly equal to Pharaoh.
Judah recalls Joseph's question about father or brother. This is his retelling, not a new direct interrogation in the current scene; the ordinary deferential address remains human.

The aged father, younger child of old age, dead brother, sole remaining maternal son and father's love are distinct claims. The reported death reflects the brothers' account rather than the narrator's knowledge.
The selected Greek promise is I will care for him. It is retained rather than replaced by an alternate set-eyes-on expression. The statement belongs to Judah's retrospective quotation.
The lad's inability to leave and the resulting he will die leave a pronoun ambiguity. The candidate does not silently name father or son as that clause's subject; context and syntax require review.
Joseph's reported condition forbids further audience without the youngest. The add/again expression is naturally no more; face remains the audience image.
Judah recounts their ascent to their father and report of the lord's words. Father is simultaneously described deferentially as your servant; the relationships are not collapsed.
The father's request repeats going again and purchasing a little food. The concise recalled command remains separate from the brothers' explanation of why they cannot comply alone.
They distinguish inability to descend alone from willingness if the youngest accompanies them. The audience condition is repeated as the cause, preserving the layered negotiation.
The father says his wife bore him two sons. It is his focused statement concerning that wife, not a narrator's denial of the other sons or wives.
The selected Greek says you said the son was beast-devoured, not I said. The plural addressees' responsibility for the report and the father's continued absence of sight remain.
This quoted warning explicitly conditions loss and sickness on taking the remaining son away. Unlike 42:38, the if-construction is present here; it is retained with old age, sorrow and Hades.
Judah sets up return without the lad and explains the father's life as hanging upon the lad's life. The suspended-life image is retained; the sentence deliberately continues into its consequence.

The father's seeing the lad absent leads to his death and the servants bringing his old age to Hades in anguish. The repeated deferential father identification remains, without inventing an immediate medical cause.

Judah recalls his guarantee to return and present the lad, with lifelong guilt otherwise. The perfect undertaking supports an ongoing responsibility; the original pledge is not reduced to a casual promise.
Judah offers himself as substitute household slave while the lad goes with his brothers. Instead of is explicit; the exchange is not softened into temporary service or generalized symbolism.
He asks how to return without the lad and seeks not to see his father's calamity. The final purpose is rendered as a plea, with the feared evils left unspecific rather than expanded.
